output.query: Organophosphate poisoning: antidotes, airway management, seizures and intermediate syndrome

results.finding: Organophosphorus pesticide poisoning is treated with resuscitation, atropine titrated to clear the chest of secretions with heart rate and blood pressure as further targets, and oxygen; pralidoxime is widely used, but trial evidence of benefit is uncertain [Eddleston_2008].
Tachycardia is common in organophosphorus poisoning because of hypoxia and nicotinic stimulation and is not a reason to withhold atropine [Eddleston_2008].
Succinylcholine is metabolized by butyrylcholinesterase, so its neuromuscular block is prolonged after organophosphorus exposure [Eddleston_2008]; mivacurium shares this pathway.

The intermediate syndrome, weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs, cranial nerves and respiratory muscles, appears 1 to 4 days after exposure and can cause respiratory failure after an apparent recovery [Eddleston_2008].

Seizures in organophosphorus poisoning are treated with benzodiazepines [Eddleston_2008]; electrographic status epilepticus is defined as seizures for 10 continuous minutes or more than 20 percent of any 60-minute period [ACNS_2021].

output.summary: Atropine, oxygen and benzodiazepines are the core of organophosphorus poisoning treatment, with uncertain evidence for oximes; butyrylcholinesterase-metabolized paralytics are avoided, and the intermediate syndrome is anticipated over the following days.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not use succinylcholine or mivacurium for intubation: butyrylcholinesterase inhibition prolongs the paralysis for hours [Eddleston_2008].
Do not withhold or reduce atropine because of tachycardia: titrate it to the chest secretions [Eddleston_2008].
Do not use fosphenytoin or phenytoin while he is hypotensive; benzodiazepines are first line for organophosphate seizures [Eddleston_2008].
Do not extubate before the intermediate syndrome has been excluded by neck flexion, proximal limb and respiratory muscle strength [Eddleston_2008].
Do not give physostigmine or neostigmine: they are cholinesterase inhibitors and worsen the poisoning.
required_recommendations: Decontaminate: remove and bag his clothing and wash the skin and hair with soap and water, with staff wearing gloves and gowns [Eddleston_2008].

Give IV atropine now, 1 to 2 mg as a rapid bolus, doubling the dose every 5 minutes until the chest is clear of secretions and wheeze, heart rate is above 80 and systolic pressure above 80 mmHg, then an infusion of 10 to 20 percent of the loading dose per hour; tachycardia of 128 is not a reason to withhold it [Eddleston_2008].
Give pralidoxime early, before the inhibited enzyme ages: 30 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes, then 8 mg/kg/h (WHO regimen), recognizing that the evidence of benefit is uncertain [Eddleston_2008].

Intubate for airway protection, bronchorrhea and hypoxemia (SpO2 88%, pO2 64 on high-flow oxygen) using rocuronium, not succinylcholine, and ventilate to correct the respiratory component of the acidosis [Eddleston_2008].

Give a benzodiazepine now for the electrographic status epilepticus: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once) or IV diazepam 0.15-0.2 mg/kg (maximum 10 mg per dose) [Glauser_2016; Eddleston_2008].

If seizures continue after the benzodiazepine, load levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid fosphenytoin because of the hypotension of 94/56; escalate to a midazolam infusion under continuous EEG if seizures persist [ESETT_2019; Brophy_2012].
Replace potassium (2.8 mEq/L) and keep magnesium in the high normal range, given the QTc of 492 ms, and avoid QT-prolonging drugs.
Give IV isotonic fluids for rhabdomyolysis with a raised creatinine (CK 8640, creatinine 1.6), monitoring urine output, potassium, creatinine and CK, and the chest for fluid overload.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

Admit to the ICU with poison center or toxicology input, and anticipate the intermediate syndrome over the next 1 to 4 days: check neck flexion, proximal and cranial nerve strength and respiratory mechanics daily before any extubation [Eddleston_2008].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
An ambulatory Holter adds nothing: the QTc and rhythm are on the 12-lead ECG, and ICU telemetry is part of management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
No structural work-up is needed acutely: the toxic cause is clear and the CT is normal; MRI may be considered later if the encephalopathy persists.

patient.chief_complaint: Found unresponsive on a campus sidewalk with twitching of the face and limbs, pinpoint pupils and copious oral secretions

family_history: Unknown: family lives in another country

social_history.note: Graduate student, lives in university dorms. Researches organophosphate compounds in neurophysiology lab. No known drug use per emergency contact. International student from China.

patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old Asian male graduate student was found unresponsive on a university campus sidewalk at 07:30 by a passerby who called 911. A laboratory colleague last saw him well at 22:00 the previous evening. EMS found him supine and unresponsive, drenched in sweat, with vomitus on his clothes and urinary incontinence; temperature 38.4 C (rectal), heart rate 128, blood pressure 94/56, respiratory rate 28 with audible gurgling and wheeze, SpO2 88% on room air, pupils pinpoint. They noted continuous irregular twitching of the face and limbs and, every few minutes, rhythmic jerking of both arms. EMS gave high-flow oxygen and suctioned the airway; no medication was given before arrival. His phone's emergency contact identified him as a neuroscience graduate student whose experiments involve handling organophosphate compounds; she knew of no drug use. A search of his backpack found an open container of an organophosphate compound used in his neurophysiology laboratory; the time and route of exposure are not known. In the ED he remains unresponsive with secretions that need suction every few minutes. Between continuous fine twitching of the face, chest wall and calves, he has recurrent episodes of eyelid flutter with rhythmic jerking of both arms lasting about a minute.

neurological_exam.additional: Copious oral and bronchial secretions requiring suction every few minutes; diffuse wheeze and coarse crackles bilaterally. Drenching sweat, lacrimation, urinary and fecal incontinence. Skin wet and not flushed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 1.5 mm bilaterally, round, minimally reactive to light. Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. Oculocephalic reflex present. Weak gag reflex with secretions pooling in the oropharynx.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 3 (E1 V1 M1): no eye opening, verbal or motor response to pain.
neurological_exam.motor: Continuous fine, irregular and asynchronous twitching of the face, chest wall and calves, with visible fasciculations. Every few minutes, rhythmic jerking of both arms with eyelid flutter for about a minute. Diffuse hypotonia between episodes. No localizing response.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Symmetrically reduced deep tendon reflexes bilaterally. Bilateral plantar responses extensor.
